Pick a dataset and a year. Each region is coloured by how that year compares
with the region's own normal, so a dark British Columbia and a dark Southern
California both mean an unusual year there, not the same number of hectares
or millimetres. The strip under the slider shows every winter: amber for an
El Niño winter, a second amber for a strong one, steel blue for La Niña,
white for a neutral winter. Click
a cell to go to that year. The ocean around the regions, and the strip of
the tropical Pacific under the map, show that winter's sea-surface
temperature. They are a picture of the winter, not an input to anything
on this site.

::: {.column-body-outset}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from pathlib import Path
print("```{=html}\n" + Path("../results/figures/region_map.html").read_text("utf-8") + "\n```")
```
:::

**How to read a year.** Year Y means the winter from December Y−1 to
February Y, the snowpack on 1 April Y, and the summer and fire season of Y.
So 1998 shows the 1997-98 El Niño winter and the fire season that followed
it.

**What the map does not show.** No trend and no test result: for those, see
[Methods and limitations](methods.qmd). Each region is a whole state,
province or territory, so one colour covers wet coasts and dry interiors
alike.
